questions.q: Why is lower-casing harmful for some tasks?
options: It removes signals such as proper nouns and acronyms ("US" vs "us") that tasks like NER rely on
It breaks Unicode encoding
It makes tokenisation slower
It changes the length of the text
questions.why: Case often carries meaning. Modern subword models usually keep case and let the model learn when it matters.

questions.q: What does Unicode NFKC normalisation do to the ligature "ﬁ"?
options: Leaves it unchanged
Replaces it with the two letters "f" and "i"
Deletes it
Converts it to uppercase
questions.why: Compatibility normalisation maps visually equivalent forms (ligatures, full-width characters) to canonical ones, so the same word always tokenises the same way.

questions.q: When padding a batch for a transformer, what must accompany the padded IDs?
options: A reversed copy of each sequence
A larger learning rate
A separate vocabulary for pad tokens
An attention mask so real tokens don't attend to pad positions and pads are left out of the loss
questions.why: Without a mask, pad tokens change the attention output of real tokens. In the loss they are usually given label -100 or masked out.

questions.q: For a decoder-only model generating text in a batch, which side is usually padded?
options: Both sides equally
The right, as for classification
The left, so every sequence's last real token sits at the final position where generation continues
Neither: decoders can't be batched
questions.why: Generation appends to the end. With left padding, the next-token logits for every row come from the same final position.

questions.q: What is the main difference between stemming and lemmatisation?
options: They give the same result for all English words
Lemmatisation only removes prefixes
Stemming chops suffixes by rule and may produce non-words; lemmatisation maps to a dictionary form using the word's part of speech
Stemming is slower but more accurate
questions.why: A Porter stemmer turns "studies" into "studi". A lemmatiser gives "study", and can map "better" to "good" when told it's an adjective.

questions.q: Why is splitting sentences on every "." unreliable?
options: It cannot handle lowercase letters
Periods are removed during normalisation
Sentences never end with a period
Periods also appear in abbreviations, decimals and initials ("Dr.", "3.14", "J. Smith")
questions.why: Sentence segmenters use rules or learned models that look at the next character's case, known abbreviation lists and context.

questions.q: What is the Levenshtein distance between "kitten" and "sitting"?
questions.why: Substitute k→s, substitute e→i, and insert g. Dynamic programming over a (7 × 8) table gives this in O(mn) time.

questions.q: Why do subword tokenisers largely remove the out-of-vocabulary problem?
options: Any word can be split into smaller known pieces, down to single characters or bytes
They map unknown words to their nearest neighbour
They have an unlimited vocabulary
They drop rare words before training
questions.why: A rare word like "detokenisation" becomes pieces such as "de", "token", "isation". Byte-level BPE can encode any string at all.

questions.q: What information does a bag-of-words representation throw away?
options: The vocabulary size
How often each word appears
Which words appear
Word order
questions.why: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" get the same vector. N-grams recover some local order at the cost of a much larger feature space.

questions.q: In TF-IDF, why does a word that appears in every document get a weight near zero?
options: TF-IDF only counts rare words
Its inverse document frequency is log(N/N), which is 0
It is removed as a stop word first
Its term frequency is zero
questions.why: IDF measures how much a word narrows down which document you're in. A word in every document tells you nothing, whatever its count.

questions.q: Why is cosine similarity usually preferred over the dot product for comparing embeddings?
options: It is faster to compute
It ignores vector length, which often reflects frequency or text length rather than meaning
It works only on positive vectors
The dot product can't be computed for dense vectors
questions.why: Cosine divides by both norms, so it compares direction only. Many embedding models normalise outputs so the two coincide.

questions.q: A bigram model saw "the cat" 3 times and "the" 10 times. With no smoothing, what is P(cat | the)?
questions.why: The maximum-likelihood estimate is count("the cat")/count("the") = 3/10. Smoothing would move some probability to unseen bigrams.

questions.q: What does skip-gram word2vec train to predict?
options: The next sentence
The document label
The context words around each centre word
The centre word from the average of its context
questions.why: Skip-gram predicts context from the centre word; CBOW does the reverse. Negative sampling replaces the full softmax with a few binary classifications.

questions.q: What does GloVe fit that word2vec does not directly use?
options: The global word co-occurrence matrix, by regressing dot products onto log co-occurrence counts
Sentence labels
A recurrent network
Character n-grams
questions.why: GloVe minimises a weighted least-squares loss on $w_i^\top \tilde w_j + b_i + \tilde b_j - \log X_{ij}$ over the whole co-occurrence table.

questions.q: How does fastText produce a vector for a word it never saw in training?
options: By using the vector of the most frequent word
By returning a zero vector
It can't; it raises an error
By summing the vectors of the word's character n-grams
questions.why: Each word is represented as its n-grams plus the whole word, so morphologically related or misspelled words still get sensible vectors.

questions.q: A common simple way to get a sentence embedding from a transformer is mean pooling. What must you be careful about?
options: Include the padding so all sentences have the same length
Normalise before the transformer, not after
Use only the last token's vector
Exclude padding positions from the mean using the attention mask
questions.why: Averaging over pads dilutes the embedding and makes it depend on how much padding the batch added.

questions.q: In BIO tagging, what does the tag "I-PER" directly after "O" signal?
options: An invalid sequence under strict BIO, since an entity must start with B
The end of a location
The start of a person entity
A token outside any entity
questions.why: Strict decoders either repair it to B-PER or forbid the transition. A CRF layer learns transition scores that make such sequences unlikely.

questions.q: Why can greedy left-to-right tagging give worse sequences than Viterbi decoding?
options: Greedy picks the best tag at each step without considering how it constrains later tags
Greedy tagging ignores emissions
Viterbi uses a larger model
Greedy is only for classification
questions.why: Viterbi finds the highest-scoring full sequence under the transition and emission scores by dynamic programming. Greedy can commit early to a tag that makes the rest worse.

questions.q: Part-of-speech tagging of "book" in "book a flight" needs what kind of information?
options: The document's topic
The surrounding context, since "book" can be a noun or a verb
Only the word's spelling
The word's frequency in the corpus
questions.why: Many words are ambiguous between categories. Here the following determiner "a" points to a verb.

questions.q: For a text classifier on very imbalanced classes, why can accuracy be misleading?
options: Accuracy can't be computed on text
Predicting the majority class for everything can score high accuracy while missing every minority example
Accuracy always equals F1
Accuracy is undefined for more than two classes
questions.why: With 95% negatives, always predicting negative gives 95% accuracy. Report per-class precision, recall and F1 or a macro average.

questions.q: An autoregressive language model factorises $P(w_1, \ldots, w_T)$ as what?
options: $\prod_t P(w_t)$
$\prod_t P(w_t \mid w_{<t})$
$\prod_t P(w_t \mid w_{t+1})$
questions.why: The chain rule is exact. The modelling assumption is how the conditional is computed: an n-gram window, an RNN state or full attention over the prefix.

questions.q: In training a transformer LM, inputs and targets are related how?
options: Targets are the same as inputs at the same position
Targets are the inputs reversed
Targets are the inputs shifted left by one position
Targets are a random mask of the inputs
questions.why: Position t predicts token t+1. A causal mask stops position t from seeing tokens after it.

questions.q: A noisy-channel spell corrector chooses the correction $c$ for typo $w$ that maximises what?
options: The edit distance between $w$ and $c$
$P(w \mid c)\,P(c)$: how likely the typo is given the word, times how common the word is
$P(c)$ alone
questions.why: By Bayes' rule, $\arg\max_c P(c \mid w) = \arg\max_c P(w \mid c) P(c)$. The error model is often based on edit operations and the prior on word frequency.

questions.q: Why does a bidirectional encoder suit NER better than a left-to-right LM?
options: It can generate text
It has fewer parameters
It doesn't need labelled data
Each token's label can depend on words after it as well as before
questions.why: In "Washington announced", whether "Washington" is a person, place or organisation may depend on later context.

questions.q: In BERT's masked-language-model training, 15% of tokens are selected. What happens to them?
options: They are deleted from the input
All become [MASK], and the loss is on every position
80% become [MASK], 10% a random token, 10% stay unchanged; the loss is computed only on the selected positions
They are replaced by the next token
questions.why: Not always using [MASK] reduces the mismatch with fine-tuning, where [MASK] never appears.

questions.q: What did later work (such as RoBERTa) find about BERT's next-sentence-prediction objective?
options: It doubled training speed
It was essential for all tasks
It should replace masked language modelling
Removing it did not hurt, and could help, downstream performance
questions.why: NSP was too easy to solve with topic cues. RoBERTa trained on longer contiguous text without it and matched or beat BERT.

questions.q: A word is split into three subword tokens for NER. A common labelling choice is what?
options: Label the first subword and ignore the rest in the loss (label -100)
Drop the word from training
Label only the last subword and the [CLS] token
Give each subword a different entity type
questions.why: This keeps one prediction per word. An alternative is to label all subwords with I- tags after the first.

questions.q: How does a span-extraction QA model choose the answer?
options: It picks the sentence with the most overlap with the question
It predicts start and end logits per token and picks the highest-scoring valid pair with start ≤ end
It generates the answer token by token
It classifies the whole passage
questions.why: Valid pairs are also limited to a maximum length and to tokens inside the context, not the question.

questions.q: Why does beam search often add a length normalisation term?
options: Raw log-probability sums favour shorter outputs, since every extra token adds a negative term
It makes beams run in parallel
Beam search can't stop otherwise
It removes repetition
questions.why: Dividing by length (or a power of it) puts hypotheses of different lengths on a fairer footing.

questions.q: What does top-p (nucleus) sampling with p = 0.9 do?
options: Samples from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities sum to at least 0.9
Scales logits by 0.9
Keeps tokens with probability above 0.9
Samples from the 90 most likely tokens
questions.why: The candidate set adapts: it is small when the model is confident and large when it is unsure. Top-k uses a fixed count instead.

questions.q: What does a temperature below 1 do to sampling?
options: Flattens it toward uniform
Sharpens the distribution toward the most likely tokens
Has no effect on argmax decoding but flattens sampling
Removes the softmax
questions.why: Logits are divided by T before softmax. T → 0 approaches greedy decoding; T > 1 gives more diverse, less reliable text.

questions.q: Why is greedy decoding prone to repetitive loops in long generations?
options: Greedy decoding ignores the prompt
It samples randomly
It always picks the end-of-sequence token
Once a phrase becomes likely, repeating it can keep it the most likely continuation at each step
questions.why: Repetition penalties, sampling or n-gram blocking are common fixes.

questions.q: A model's average per-token cross-entropy is 2.0 nats. What is its perplexity?
options: $\log 2$
$e^2 \approx 7.39$
questions.why: Perplexity is the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood. Perplexities are only comparable between models that use the same tokenizer.

questions.q: Why can't perplexities of models with different tokenizers be compared directly?
options: Only character models have perplexity
Perplexity always increases with vocabulary size by exactly the log ratio
Perplexity is undefined for subword models
Per-token loss depends on how the text is split; a tokenizer with longer tokens has fewer, harder predictions
questions.why: Convert to a tokenizer-independent measure, such as bits per byte or per character, before comparing.

questions.q: What does MinHash estimate between two documents?
options: The cosine of their embeddings
The Jaccard similarity of their shingle sets
Their edit distance
Their perplexity under a reference model
questions.why: The probability that two sets have the same minimum hash equals their Jaccard similarity. LSH banding over many hashes finds near-duplicate pairs without comparing every pair.

questions.q: BLEU is built mainly on what?
options: Embedding similarity
Human ratings
Modified n-gram precision against references, times a brevity penalty
Recall of reference unigrams only
questions.why: Clipped precision for n = 1 to 4 is combined by a geometric mean. The brevity penalty stops very short outputs from scoring high precision.

questions.q: ROUGE-L is based on what?
options: Word embedding overlap
Bigram precision
The longest common substring only
The longest common subsequence between candidate and reference
questions.why: LCS allows gaps, so it rewards matching words in the same order without needing them to be contiguous.

questions.q: One BPE training step does what?
options: Counts adjacent symbol pairs across the corpus and merges the most frequent pair into a new symbol
Removes the rarest character
Splits the longest word in half
Picks the token with the highest likelihood gain under a unigram model
questions.why: Repeating the merge until the vocabulary reaches its target size gives an ordered merge list. Encoding applies merges in the same order.

questions.q: How does a unigram LM tokenizer (as in SentencePiece) differ from BPE at training time?
options: It starts from characters and merges pairs
It uses no probabilities
It starts with a large vocabulary and removes pieces that least reduce corpus likelihood
It works only on whitespace-split words
questions.why: BPE builds up by merging; unigram prunes down. Unigram also allows sampling several segmentations of the same text for regularisation.

questions.q: A ranking system returns relevant documents at positions 1 and 3 of five. What is its reciprocal rank for this query?
questions.why: Reciprocal rank uses only the first relevant result, here at position 1. Metrics like MAP or NDCG also account for the second relevant document.
